input.original_title: Big Beautiful Bill: Pass-Through Deduction Permanently Slashes Taxes for Trump-Style Owners

existing.title: Big Beautiful Bill: Pass-Through Deduction Permanently Slashes Taxes for Trump-Style Owners
existing.description_short: Big Beautiful Bill: Pass-Through Deduction Permanently Slashes Taxes for Trump-Style Owners
existing.description_long: On July 4, 2025, President Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law — a $3.4 trillion deficit-expanding tax package per Congressional Budget Office estimates. Among its most significant provisions for Trump and his class of business owners was the permanent extension of the 20% pass-through business income deduction (Section 199A), which reduces effective marginal tax rates on passive business income by more than 20% compared with rates on ordinary wages. In 2022, 87% of pass-through deduction benefits went to the top 10% of Americans by income, and half went to millionaires. The bill also permanently doubled estate tax exemptions to $15 million per person (a $212 billion cost through 2034). The real estate industry received specific loosened restrictions on real estate investment trusts. The SALT deduction cap was raised to $40,400 for those earning under $500,000 from 2025 to 2029, and critically, the final bill retained the pass-through entity SALT workaround — allowing wealthy real estate and business owners to fully deduct state and local taxes at the entity level, circumventing the individual SALT cap. Pass-through SALT limits that would have raised $37 billion were stripped from the final bill. Trump's own business empire, structured entirely through pass-through entities, stands to benefit across every one of these provisions. Democrats noted the bill contained virtually no provisions specifically designed to benefit middle-class or working Americans on a permanent basis.

input.original_title: Anti-Journalist Violence Rallies - Celebrating Reporter's Injury

existing.title: Anti-Journalist Violence Rallies - Celebrating Reporter's Injury
existing.description_short: Anti-Journalist Violence Rallies - Celebrating Reporter's Injury
existing.description_long: Donald Trump turned his campaign rallies into celebrations of violence against journalists, repeatedly telling crowds how 'beautiful' it was when MSNBC correspondent Ali Velshi was hit by a rubber bullet while covering racial justice protests, demonstrating his dangerous encouragement of anti-media violence. At rallies in Minnesota and North Carolina, Trump inaccurately recounted Velshi being struck by what he falsely claimed was a tear gas canister, calling the injury 'the most beautiful thing' and 'law and order.' Trump's celebration of a journalist's injury while doing his job represented an unprecedented presidential encouragement of violence against the press, escalating his anti-media rhetoric from calling them 'enemy of the people' to actively celebrating their physical harm. The attacks on Velshi came as Trump had already created a dangerous climate for journalists at his rallies, where supporters regularly hurled insults and made threatening gestures toward reporters in the press pen. A BBC cameraman was shoved by a Trump supporter at an El Paso rally, while Trump's anti-media rhetoric contributed to an atmosphere where violence against journalists was normalized and celebrated. Trump's specific targeting of Velshi by name while celebrating his injury crossed a dangerous line from rhetoric to active incitement of violence, with press freedom organizations warning about the grave threat to journalist safety. The celebration of Velshi's injury demonstrated Trump's complete abandonment of presidential norms protecting press freedom, using a journalist's pain as rally entertainment while encouraging future violence against media covering his events.

context.synopsis: The United States experienced its largest measles resurgence since 1992 in 2025, with 2,289 confirmed cases across 45 states — a more than 8-fold increase over 2024's 285 cases. The outbreak, centered in Gaines County, West Texas, killed two unvaccinated children in Lubbock with no underlying health conditions, and one adult in New Mexico — the first U.S. measles deaths in over a decade. Overall hospitalization rates reached 11–13%, with children under 5 hospitalized at a 23% rate. Experts cited declining vaccination rates (92.7% kindergarten MMR coverage, below the 95% herd immunity threshold) and RFK Jr.'s anti-vaccine messaging as contributing factors; by August 2026, cases had risen to 2,465 across 47 states.
context.recovered_rationale: This matters because the documented measles resurgence produced deaths, substantial hospitalization, and spread across much of the country, while vaccination coverage fell below the stated herd-immunity threshold. The record indicates a public-health protection gap affecting children especially severely and identifies anti-vaccine messaging as a contributing concern, making prevention capacity and official health communication central accountability issues.
